name: Proto-Southeast Barito
region: Central and South Kalimantan, east of the Barito river; Madagascar
orthography_note: Adelaar (2012) writes PSEB e for the mid front vowel that continues both the PMP schwa and final *a (*katen 'itchy' < *katəl, *rue 'two' < *duSa); Adelaar (1995: 340), after Hudson (1967), calls it 'a mid-front vowel'. Mahdi (1988) writes ɛ in *-ɛy.
notes: The language ancestral to Malagasy and to the Southeast Barito languages of Kalimantan (Ma'anyan, Samihim, Paku, Dusun Witu and others: Hudson 1967; Dahl 1951, 1977), 'spoken along the eastern shores of the Barito River in Central Kalimantan Province, and in a few disconnected areas in South Kalimantan' (Adelaar 2012: 124 n. 4). Its changes are premigratory and attested in the SEB languages of Kalimantan (Table 3, p. 131). Adelaar (2012: 132 n. 12) finds Ma'anyan and Samihim mutually understandable dialects 'more closely related to MLG than other forms of SEB'; Mahdi (1988) puts Malagasy as a separate branch at equal distance from the other SEB languages (Adelaar 1991: 8). Adelaar (2013: 467) places the split of Proto-East Barito into PSEB and Proto-Central East Barito before the *li > di and *ti > tsi tendencies. Ma'anyan and Dusun Witu stay under Proto-Barito with Smith's (2017a) rows (decision adelaar2012-pseb). PAN etyma are restated against PMP (Proto-Barito inherits the PMP inventory).
inherit_note: Phonemes for which no source states a change (p, t, k, m, n, ŋ, ɲ, l, a, i, u, w) are carried down from Proto-Barito unchanged.

name: Proto-Malagasy
orthography_note: Adelaar's (2012, 2013) PMLG forms are not consistent in the stops and glides: *fitu, *afu, *lelef-an and *hali, *hatuk beside *katen, *wulan, *waye (2012: 127, 130, 135-136). The rows enter *p > f and *k > h at this stage, *w > v in the dialects.
notes: 'Any stage after SEB speakers had sailed to East Africa' (Adelaar 2012: 135 n. 27); the changes of Table 4 (p. 135) are postmigratory. All three final nasals *-m, *-n, *-ŋ were still distinct, as Flacourt's (1658) Old South Betsimisaraka shows (p. 137). Adelaar (2012: §§3-5, 7) ascribes the spirantization of stops, the fricativization of the semivowels, the paragogic vowels, the affricate tr and the reduction of nasal + stop clusters to contact with Sabaki (Comorian) and Makhuwa after the migration; the settlers reached Madagascar from the East African coast as a mixed Austronesian-Bantu population (pp. 145-146; Adelaar 2013: 477). Dialect classification is left open (decision adelaar2013-classification).
inherit_note: Phonemes for which no source states a change are carried down from PSEB unchanged.

name: Plateau Malagasy
notes: Glottolog's language for Merina, Betsileo, Antaimoro and other central varieties; entered as the node of Merina, the dialect the sources cite.

name: Merina
region: Imerina, the central highlands around Antananarivo
orthography_note: IPA. Adelaar writes the orthography with o as u: tr = ʈ͡ʂ, ts = t͡s, z = z, y (final) = i, and marks the paragogic (whispered) vowel with a breve (-tră, -kă, -nă). Final -tr, -k and -n are entered as the consonant; the paragogic vowel is in the notes.
notes: The dialect on which Standard Malagasy is based; 'not only the dominant dialect but ... also one of the most innovative of all Malagasy dialects' (Adelaar 2013: 473). Historical final consonants merged as -tră, -kă, -nă or were lost; before a vowel-initial suffix other consonants can reappear (-tră/-r-, -t-, -f-; -kă/-f-, -h-; -nă/-m-), by the rules of Mahdi (1988: 241-262) (Adelaar 2012: 124-125). Stress is contrastive on any of the last three syllables (MLG3, p. 137). Data from Webber (1853), Richardson (1885) and Abinal & Malzac (Adelaar 2012: 155).

name: Sakalava
region: West coast of Madagascar around Morondava
orthography_note: IPA; the paragogic vowel is -ĕ (Adelaar 2012: 128 n. 8).
notes: Adelaar (2012) calls it South Sakalava (SSK), from Gueunier (n.d.); Adelaar (2013: 461) uses 'Sakalava' for the dialect of Morondava and thereabout, a western dialect, and keeps South Sakalava and North Sakalava apart: 'the northern and southern dialects appear to be less akin to one another than to other nearby dialects' (2012: 155). It has lost all final nasals but keeps *-t and *-k (2012: 128); it still distinguishes final *-i and *-e (2012: 136; 2013: 474, Table 8). Sakalava and Tandroy have productive ni- and <in> marking past tense (2013: 476).

name: North Sakalava
notes: Adelaar's NSK, from Thomas-Fattier (1982) (2012: 155). A northern dialect, 'more similar to Tsimihety and Tankarana' than to Sakalava of Morondava (2013: 461). Glottolog 5.4 has no languoid for it (decision adelaar2012-dialects). The paragoge echoes the vowel of the preceding syllable, and original final nasals are often not followed by a vowel (2012: 130).

name: Bara
notes: From Elli (1988) (Adelaar 2012: 155). The paragogic vowel is -ĭ (2012: 130). Western varieties of Bara belong to the western dialects, eastern Bara to the central ones (2013: 458, 461).

name: Tandroy
notes: From Rajaonarimanana & Fee (1996) (Adelaar 2012: 155-156). A southwestern dialect (2013: 458). Has no locative voice but an instrumental and an applicative voice (2013: 476).

name: Tankarana
notes: Adelaar (2013: 463-464, Table 3) compares three subdialects (Ambiloha, Antalaha, Vohemar) from Serva & Petroni's (2011) lists. A northern dialect; Vérin, Kottak & Gorlin (1969) make it a primary branch.

name: Tsimihety
notes: Data from Faridanona (1977) and Hideo Fukazawa (Adelaar 2013: 464-465, Table 4). A northern dialect; Vérin, Kottak & Gorlin (1969) make it a primary branch.

name: South Betsimisaraka
region: Central and southern east coast of Madagascar
notes: From Ruud (1955) (Adelaar 2012: 155; 2013 cites pages as R47 etc.). 'Betsimisaraka' covers several subdialects along a long stretch of the east coast and 'needs to be defined more clearly' (2013: 467, 477). Ruud's final r 'must be a retroflex affricate' (2013: 463, Table 2 note). Adelaar (2012) also cites Flacourt's (1658) dictionary as Old South Betsimisaraka; in 2013 (p. 466) he treats Flacourt as a Tanosy source (decision adelaar2012-dialects).

name: Tanosy
region: South-east coast of Madagascar around Tolanaro (Fort-Dauphin)
notes: An eastern dialect (Adelaar 2013: 458). Dez (1963) has Tanosy as the only dialect with *ti > tsi but *li kept; current Tanosy has many di and tsi forms from standard Malagasy (2013: 465-466 and n. 6). Flacourt's (1658) dictionary was compiled around Fort-Dauphin (2013: 466).

name: Old South East Malagasy
notes: The language of the oldest Malagasy literature, in Sorabe (Arabic) script, 'an old form of coastal South East Malagasy'; 'often incorrectly assumed to be an old form of Taimoro' (Adelaar 2013: 458 n. 2), as Adelaar (2012) still calls it (Old Taimoro). Data from a sixteenth-century text in Ferrand (1904), cited with page numbers (F114 etc.). Sorabe writes tr as a geminated r sign (2012: 141 n. 38); vowels are diacritics, so a written waw or yod marks a semivowel or a long vowel (2012: 139 n. 34). An attested historical variety, entered as a language with no Glottocode (decision adelaar2012-dialects).
